newsitem.title: COSTA RICA: Rich nations faulted as not preserving ozone layer.
newsitem.headline: Rich nations faulted as not preserving ozone layer.

text.p: Non-governmental environmental organisations on Tuesday accused five of the world's wealthiest countries of failing to boost funding to help preserve the threatened ozone layer.

At a news conference during a three-day gathering to discuss the ozone layer, the environmental groups said France, Australia, Canada, Japan and the United States were resisting attempts to increase funding.
The groups said the additional funding would allow developing nations to get rid of the destructive substances.

"France in particular has given a clear message that it will not increase its funding, saying that it has reached a funding ceiling and is not interested in negotiating," said Corinna Gilfillan, of the U.S. branch of the Friends of the Earth.
Gilfillan said the United States is responsible for 30 percent of the total production of chemicals that destroy the ozone layer and has a responsibility to increase financing.
The conference, which started Monday and ends Wednesday, brought together about 800 delegates from 164 countries.

The three-day meeting was marked by a dispute between wealthy and developing nations over how much to spend to safeguard the ozone layer, which shields the Earth from ultraviolet radiation associated with cancer in humans.

"What has remained outside of the debate on funding are considerations about environmental, economic and health costs that follow from the destruction of the ozone layer," said Lucas Kodzo Agbanaglo, with Friends of the Earth in Togo.

The 1987 Montreal Protocol, ratified by at least 150 countries, called for the gradual phasing out of ozone depleting substances and established the Multilateral Fund to encourage technology transfer and a switch to environmentally friendly substances.
